claims.text: on-call.md @ stage-4: paging is a plan, not live; the rotation is the team's four developers, one-week shifts; each shift has a primary and a secondary (the next shift's person); each developer is primary one week in four plus one secondary week.

on-call-staffing.md lines 11-12: at least five people before a rotation pages outside working hours (for every severity: page alert, per lines 23-24); with one-week shifts nobody is primary more than one week in five.

on-call-staffing.md lines 14-21: with four developers, until a second team forms, only SEV1 pages outside working hours; SEV2 alerts firing outside hours are handled at the start of the next working hours; during working hours paging follows on-call.md.

incident-response.md: SEV1 is the highest severity, order placement fails for every shop; SEV2 is any other severity: page alert firing (S2-S4, or S1 when only part of orders fail); the on-call person sets severity when acknowledging the page.
on-call-staffing.md lines 23-24: when teams split under ADR 0025, each new rotation must have five people before paging outside working hours for every severity: page alert.

on-call-staffing.md lines 6-7: every number in the document is the project's assumed policy, reviewed after three months of real on-call; the document was written after on-call.md and incident-response.md and does not replace them (lines 3-6).

on-call-staffing.md lines 28-40: fairness is load, not shift count; monthly the team lead counts per person pages (useless ones too), night pages (22:00-07:00), weekend or holiday shifts, swaps (given and taken); the clearly most loaded gets fewer weekend shifts next month; counts never rate anyone.

on-call-staffing.md lines 44-47: a person paged at night starts late the next day without asking; a shift with more than two night pages puts reducing those alerts (fix cause, fix threshold, or lower to ticket) at the top of the next sprint, before feature work.

on-call-staffing.md lines 58-65: rules apply from the day paging runs for real; no notifier exists today, so the schedule serves drills only; pay or time off for on-call is decided by the company and labour law, the document sets no amount.

claims.text: Below five, failures below SEV1 (every other page alert, i.e. SEV2) wait for working hours at night and keep burning error budget. One reading, not stated by the document: the team accepts that cost so people are rested for a SEV1; how an unanswered alert is judged SEV1 is left open.
claims.source_hint: on-call-staffing.md lines 14-21; incident-response.md severity table; alerts.md fast burn definition

claims.text: Trade-offs: four people paging for every page alert is ruled out below five; SEV1-only fits below five with no second team; five or more fits large teams or each team after the split; concentrating shifts on the most experienced fits rarely, as a short named stopgap the document does not use.

Hedged choices: a four-person Cửa hàng rotation plausibly keeps SEV1-only at night until five (document does not spell it out); show the night pages and fix size to whoever sets sprint priorities; for a persistent high count look at swaps or a recurring alert, not the person.

Piling shifts on a few wears down the people the team relies on most and gives everyone else little practice answering a page; symptoms (hedged): same names fill every count, uneven night pages behind an even calendar, the same alert paging night after night.

Try it: with the given month, B gets fewer weekend shifts (line 39); B's shift had >2 night pages so alert reduction tops the next sprint (45-47); B and C start late after night pages (44); the table must not rate anyone (40).

beyond_scope: Section 8 contrasts misconception 1 with others getting little practice answering a page; the newcomer shadow path (lines 49-56) is not taught.
